longForm.title: The Brown Water Navy: Riverine Warfare in the Mekong Delta, 1967-1969
longForm.excerpt: The Mekong Delta had no high ground and no roads that reached its interior. The only way to fight there was from the water. In 1967, the US Navy and Army built a joint riverine force to do exactly that. What they found was a Viet Cong that had been preparing for them for years.
paragraphs: The Mekong Delta has no high ground. Forty thousand square miles of waterways, rice paddies, mangrove swamp, and canal networks — the most densely populated and most strategically important agricultural region in South Vietnam. The Viet Cong had been operating in the delta since before American forces arrived in country. The terrain was theirs: every canal fork, every sampan crossing, every hamlet and treeline. The Army divisions and Marine regiments that worked in the northern provinces had no access to the delta's interior without boats. The helicopter helped, but helicopters needed landing zones, and the delta's flooded rice paddies offered few. MACV's tactical problem in 1966 was not identifying the Viet Cong in the delta — it was getting to them.

The solution was a concept that the US Navy and Army worked out jointly through 1966 and implemented beginning in early 1967: the Mobile Riverine Force, designated Task Force 117. The force was a combined Army-Navy structure with no direct precedent in American military history since the Civil War. The Navy provided the waterborne element — a flotilla of armored river assault craft operating from self-propelled barracks ships that became, effectively, floating fire bases anchored in the major waterways. The Army provided the infantry: the 2nd Brigade, 9th Infantry Division, which trained specifically for riverine operations, embarked on the Navy's craft, and assaulted objectives directly from the water. The concept was sound. The execution required solving problems that neither service had encountered in this combination before, and solving them in contact.

The riverine fleet that Task Force 117 operated was purpose-built for the delta environment. The Monitor was the fire support vessel — a converted Landing Craft, Mechanized, armored and armed with 40mm and 20mm guns, a 81mm mortar, and, in some configurations, a flamethrower. The Armored Troop Carrier was the primary assault craft: a modified LCVP with armored sides and ramps that allowed infantry to assault directly from the water onto a riverbank. The Assault Support Patrol Boat was faster and lighter, used for scouting and fire support along the flanks of assault formations. The Command and Communications Boat provided the floating headquarters that coordinated the joint operation in terrain where radio communications were degraded by vegetation and terrain features. Each class of vessel had been designed for a specific tactical function in an environment where tactical function was defined by where the water was.

The tactical problem that dominated riverine operations was the ambush. A waterway is a linear obstacle with forced movement — boats cannot maneuver laterally the way infantry can maneuver on land. The Viet Cong understood this better than the task force planners had modeled it. A classic delta ambush placed weapons on both banks of a narrow waterway, with B-40 rocket teams covering the lead and trail elements and automatic weapons covering the center. The boats had no space to maneuver, no cover to use, and nowhere to go but forward or backward — both of which the ambush was designed to suppress. The answer that the task force developed was to make the first few seconds of an ambush as destructive as possible for the attackers: all weapons on both sides of every boat firing outboard simultaneously on contact, without waiting to acquire specific targets. The volume of fire suppressed the ambush long enough for the boats to push through or to land infantry directly into the ambush position. It worked better than the alternative. It did not make river movement safe.

Task Force 116, designated Operation Game Warden, ran the Patrol Boat Riverine program on the waterways where the Mobile Riverine Force was not operating. The PBR — Patrol Boat, River, Mark I and later Mark II — was a fiberglass-hulled craft driven by water-jet propulsion rather than conventional screws, which gave it the ability to operate in extremely shallow water and to reverse direction without turning. It carried twin .50 caliber machine guns forward, a single .50 or M60 aft, and could be crewed by four men. The water-jet propulsion eliminated the vulnerability to underwater obstructions and wire that had plagued propeller-driven craft. PBRs operated in two-boat sections, conducting round-the-clock patrols, inspecting sampan traffic for contraband and infiltrators, and responding to contact reports. They were fast enough to chase most waterborne Viet Cong logistics, and they were present at a scale the larger Task Force 117 craft could not match.

The CORONADO series of operations — CORONADO I through CORONADO IX, conducted between 1967 and 1968 — were the Mobile Riverine Force's primary operational commitment in the delta. The operations targeted Viet Cong main force units in the Mekong Delta provinces, seeking to fix them in place with the river assault force and destroy them with infantry and close air support. The results were mixed in the way that search-and-destroy results were consistently mixed throughout the war: contact was made, engagements were fought, casualties were inflicted. The Viet Cong's ability to disperse into the population and to break contact when it suited them limited the operations' ability to destroy units rather than attrit them. The terrain that made helicopter extraction difficult also made infantry pursuit after contact slow and predictable. The Viet Cong got away more often than the operation's concept required them to.

The intelligence problem in the delta was more acute than in other operational environments. The delta's population density — approximately ten million people in a relatively small area — created an intelligence environment in which distinguishing Viet Cong infrastructure from civilian population required the kind of granular, locally-sourced human intelligence that the Mobile Riverine Force, a conventional military organization operating in a foreign language environment, was structurally ill-positioned to develop. The CORDS program and its Provincial Reconnaissance Units, operating through Vietnamese intermediaries, had better access to that intelligence layer. The riverine force depended on CORDS intelligence for targeting, which meant it operated at the pace CORDS could produce, not at the pace the task force's operational tempo required.

What the Mobile Riverine Force demonstrated by 1968, and what the subsequent Naval history and Army CMH studies documented, was that riverine warfare in the delta required a different force structure than had been available at the program's start. The joint Army-Navy concept worked better than either service had expected; the boat crews and the infantry developed an operational relationship that produced effective tactical results under extremely difficult conditions. The limitation was not the concept. It was that the Mekong Delta could not be controlled by conventional military means alone — that the population density, the VC infrastructure, and the terrain created a military-political problem that the task force's firepower and mobility, however well applied, could not resolve without a parallel political and governance effort. The delta was the place in Vietnam where the mismatch between the military instrument and the political problem was most visible, most consistently, and most thoroughly documented.

shortForm.title: The Ambush on the Mekong: How the Viet Cong Fought the River War
shortForm.excerpt: The Viet Cong had been fighting on the Mekong Delta's waterways since the early 1960s. Their ambush doctrine was adapted to the hydrography. When the Mobile Riverine Force arrived in 1967, they were ready.
paragraphs: The ambush geometry on a Vietnamese river canal was not improvised. The Viet Cong had been fighting on the delta's waterways since the early 1960s, and their ambush doctrine was adapted specifically to the hydrography — the width of the canals, the height of the vegetation on the banks, the distances at which B-40 rockets and RPGs were most effective against armored hulls. A standard ambush placed the main body on one bank, with a secondary position on the other bank to prevent the boats from using the far shore as cover. The primary weapons were B-40 rocket-propelled grenades, recoilless rifles for the larger craft, and automatic weapons — AK-47s and RPD machine guns — for suppressing the crews. The ambush was typically initiated by the rocket teams, with automatic weapons following immediately to prevent the crews from returning effective fire.

The tactical response that the riverine force developed was the 'mad minute' on contact — every weapon on every boat firing simultaneously outboard, into both banks, the moment an ambush was initiated. The response was not aimed fire. It was suppression: enough volume to force the ambush teams off their firing positions long enough for the boats to close the range or land infantry. The effectiveness of the response depended on crew training and crew cohesion. A boat crew that hesitated — trying to identify targets before firing — was a crew that was still taking organized fire from prepared positions while it hesitated. The crews who survived in the delta were the crews who did not hesitate. That is a training outcome, not a natural behavior, and it required sustained operational conditioning that the replacement rotation system consistently disrupted.

The Viet Cong countered the mad-minute response in two ways. The first was to initiate ambushes at ranges that made the suppression response less effective — at distances of 50 meters or less, where the ambush teams could engage through the suppression and where closing the range quickly was difficult in a narrow canal. The second was to use water mines — command-detonated and pressure-fused — at the ambush site, triggered simultaneously with the small-arms fire. A mine under or alongside an armored troop carrier changed the tactical equation significantly; the ATC could absorb RPG and automatic weapons fire, but it could not absorb a command-detonated mine under the hull. The tactical adaptation was, as in every phase of the war, an iterative process: American innovation producing a counter, Viet Cong counter-adaptation producing a response, and so on. The delta was where that iteration ran fastest because the terrain gave the Viet Cong the most consistent tactical advantage.

onThisDay.headline: Operation Little Switch Prisoner Exchange Concludes in Korea
onThisDay.body: On May 3-4, 1953, Operation Little Switch — the exchange of sick and wounded prisoners of war between the United Nations Command and Communist forces in Korea — concluded at Panmunjom, with 684 UN prisoners repatriated and 6,670 North Korean and Chinese prisoners returned. The exchange was the first significant step toward the armistice signed July 27, 1953.
